'''''Kunzea ericoides''''', commonly known as '''kānuka''' or '''white tea-tree''', is a tree or shrub in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Myrtaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to New Zealand. It has white or pink flowers similar to those of ''[[Leptospermum]]'' and from its first formal description in 1832 until 1983 was known as ''Leptospermum ericoides''. The flowers have five [[petal]]s and up to 25 [[stamen]]s which are mostly longer than the petals.

==Description==
''Kunzea ericoides'' is a spreading shrub or tree, sometimes growing to a height of {{convert|18|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} with bark which peels in long strips and young branches which tend to droop. The leaves are variable in shape from linear to narrow elliptic or lance-shaped, {{convert|6.5-25|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1-5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide with a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] up to {{convert|1|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. The flowers are white or pale pink, crowded on side branches or in the [[wikt:axil#Noun|axils]] of upper leaves. The [[Hypanthium|floral cup]] is covered with soft, downy hairs and is on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{convert|3-6|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. There are five triangular [[sepal]]s about {{convert|1|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and five petals about {{convert|2|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. There are up to 25 stamens which are {{convert|1-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}}, mostly longer than the petals. Flowering occurs between October and February and is followed by fruit which is a cup-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{convert|2-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and wide. The capsule usually opens to release its seed when mature.<ref name="NZPCN">{{cite web|last1=de Lange|first1=Peter J.|title=''Kunzea ericoides''|url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=885|publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref><ref name="PhytoKeys">{{cite journal|last1=de Lange|first1=Peter J.|title=A revision of the New Zealand ''Kunzea ericoides'' (Myrtaceae) complex|journal=PhytoKeys|date=2014|issue=40|pages=1–185|url=https://phytokeys.pensoft.net/article/1924/list/8/|access-date=13 December 2017|doi=10.3897/phytokeys.40.7973|pmid=25197228|pmc=4154306 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2014PhytK..40....1D }}</ref>

''Kunzea ericoides'' is very similar to the [[Australia]]n endemics ''[[Kunzea leptospermoides|K. leptospermoides]]'' and ''[[Kunzea peduncularis|K. peduncularis]]'' which were formerly included in ''K. ericoides''. The new status of ''K. ericoides'' follows the publication of a paper entitled "A revision of the New Zealand ''Kunzea ericoides'' ([[Myrtaceae]]) complex" by the New Zealand botanist [[Peter de Lange (botanist)|Peter de Lange]].<ref name="PhytoKeys" /><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web|last1=Messina|first1=Andre|last2=Stajsic|first2=Val|title=''Kunzea leptospermoides''|url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/f47b8df6-f97e-4757-8d11-e2a73d4df8d0|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria|access-date=14 December 2017}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Kānuka was first formally described in 1832 by the French botanist [[Achille Richard]] who gave it the name ''Leptospermum ericoides'' from a specimen he collected in New Zealand. The description was published in ''Voyage de découvertes de l'Astrolabe - Botanique''.<ref name=APNI(1)>{{cite web|title=''Leptospermum ericoides''|url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/523376|publisher=APNI|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref><ref name="Achille">{{cite book|last1=Richard|first1=Achille|title=Voyage de découvertes de l'Astrolabe. Botanique|date=1832|publisher=Henri Dupuy|location=Paris|pages=338–339|url=https://www.odsas.net/scan_sets.php?set_id=471&doc=51626|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref> In 1983, Australian botanist [[Joy Thompson]] changed the scientific name to ''Kunzea ericoides'', describing the differences between ''Leptospermum'' and ''Kunzea'' in ''[[Telopea (journal)|Telopea]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Kunzea ericoides''|url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/467736|publisher=APNI|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref><ref name="Telopea">{{cite journal|last1=Thompson|first1=Joy|title=Redefinitions and nomenclatural changes within the ''Leptospermum'' suballiance of Myrtaceae|journal=Telopea|date=1983|volume=2|issue=4|pages=379–380|doi=10.7751/telopea19834403|doi-access=free|bibcode=1983Telop...2..379T }}</ref> The [[Botanical nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''ericoides'') refers to the similarity of the habit of this species to that of ''[[Erica arborea]]''.<ref name="NZflora">{{cite web|title=''Kunzea ericoides'' (A.Rich.) Joy Thomps.|url=http://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Kunzea-ericoides.html|publisher=Landcare Research: Manaaki Whenua|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref> The [[wikt:suffix|suffix]] ''-oides'' is a [[Latin]] ending meaning "likeness".<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|author-link1=Roland W. Brown|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page =45}}</ref> The taxonomic revision of the ''Kunzea ericoides'' complex identified ten species endemic to New Zealand, seven of which were new at this time.<ref name="PhytoKeys" /> A more recent analysis of the ''Kunzea'' complex observed little genetic variation and morphological distinction between the species, questioning the evidence for ten endemic ''Kunzea'' species and suggesting further revision.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Heenan|first1=Peter B.|last2=McGlone|first2=Matt S.|last3=Mitchell|first3=Caroline M.|last4=Cheeseman|first4=Dagmar F.|last5=Houliston|first5=Gary J.|date=2021-04-07|title=Genetic variation reveals broad-scale biogeographic patterns and challenges species' classification in the Kunzea ericoides (kānuka; Myrtaceae) complex from New Zealand|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0028825X.2021.1903946|journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany|volume=60 |language=en|pages=2–26|doi=10.1080/0028825X.2021.1903946|s2cid=234860363|issn=0028-825X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Etymology===
Common names for this species include: kānuka, kōpuka, manuea, mānuka, mānuka-rauriki, mārū, rauiri, rauwiri, white tea tree,<ref name="NZflora" /> and tree manuka.<ref name="Landcare">{{cite web |title=''Kunzea ericoides'' |url=https://wtlandcare.org/details/kunzea-ericoides/ |publisher=Woolshed Thurgoona Landcare Group |access-date=14 April 2023}}</ref>

''Kānuka'' can also refer to ''[[Kunzea robusta]]'', it is a [[Doublet (linguistics)|doublet]] of ''[[Leptospermum scoparium|mānuka]]'' from [[Proto-Polynesian language|Proto-Polynesian]] ''nukanuka'' or ''nuka'' which originally refers to ''[[Decaspermum fruticosum]]'' due to its similar small white flowers.<ref name="TMR">{{cite web |title=Proto-polynesian etymologies |url=http://www.temarareo.org/PPN-Manuka.html |publisher=Te Māra Reo |access-date=4 December 2022}}</ref>

==Distribution==
Kānuka (or mānuka, as it was mostly known until the 1930s) is only known from the north of the [[South Island]]. It is found north of the [[Buller River|Buller]] and [[Wairau River]]s, and is most common near [[Nelson, New Zealand|Nelson]]. It mostly grows in [[shrubland]] and forest in coastal and lowland areas, rarely in subalpine shrubland.

Members of the kānuka complex are found throughout New Zealand occurring on the [[Three Kings Islands]], Aotea ([[Great Barrier Island]]), from Te Paki (on the [[Aupōuri Peninsula]]) at the northern tip of the [[North Island]] to as far south as [[Dunedin]] and [[Central Otago]] in the South Island, and [[Stewart Island]]. Within this range kānuka is widespread ranging from coastal scrub and sand dunes (where it may form a distinct forest type) through lowland and [[montane forest]], with one member of the complex reaching elevations of 2000 metres above sea level.

==Ecology==
Kānuka often colonizes land [[fire ecology|recovering after a fire]] and is a critical part of the natural recovery of agricultural areas and open [[disturbed ground]] to forest. With its small but abundant flowers it can colour a whole hillside white, almost giving the appearance of snow cover. The wood is very hard and although not durable in the ground it is used for wharf piles and tool handles. It is particularly popular as firewood, and burns with a great heat.

Kānuka can grow to around 10 metres high. [[Kākāriki]] [[parakeet]]s (''Cyanoramphus'') use the leaves and bark of kānuka and the related [[Leptospermum scoparium|mānuka]] tea trees to rid themselves of parasites. Apart from ingesting the material, they also chew it, mix it with [[preen gland]] oil and apply it to their feathers.<ref>Terry Greene. 1989. Antiparasitic behaviour in New Zealand parakeets ("Cyanoramphus" species). ''[[Notornis (journal)|Notornis]]'' '''36'''(4): 322–323. [http://www.notornis.org.nz/free_issues/Notornis_36-1989/Notornis_36_4.pdf PDF fulltext] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017222920/http://www.notornis.org.nz/free_issues/Notornis_36-1989/Notornis_36_4.pdf |date=2008-10-17 }}</ref> Mānuka and kānuka are superficially similar species and are often confused with one another. The easiest way to tell the difference between them is to feel the foliage, kānuka leaves being soft, while mānuka leaves are prickly.<ref>John Dawson and Rob Lucas. 2000</ref> ''K. ericoides'' may occur in the understory of certain [[rimu]]/[[nothofagus]] forests in the [[South Island]]. Typical associate [[understory]] species may include [[Lomaria discolor|crown fern]] (''Lomaria discolor'') and ''[[Cyathodes fasciculata]]''.<ref name="Hogan">{{cite web|last1=Hogan|first1=C. Michael|title=Crown Fern ''Blechnum discolor''|url=http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=95431|publisher=Globaltwitcher.com|access-date=7 July 2017|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120213134120/http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=95431|archive-date=13 February 2012}}</ref>

==Prostrate kānuka==
A [[Variety (botany)|variety]] of kānuka, the prostrate kānuka (''Kunzea ericoides'' var. ''microflora''), is one of the few plants that can survive hot ground in the immediate surroundings of [[Geothermal activity#Geothermal activity|geothermal]] features such as [[fumarole]]s and craters, for instance at "[[Craters of the Moon (geothermal site)|Craters of the Moon]]" (Karapiti), a geothermal area close to [[Taupō]], New Zealand.<ref name="Given">{{cite journal|last1=Given|first1=David R.|title=Vegetation on heated soils at Karapiti, central North Island, New Zealand, and its relation to ground|journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany|date=1980|volume=18|issue=1 |pages=1–13|doi=10.1080/0028825x.1980.10427227|doi-access=free|bibcode=1980NZJB...18....1G }}</ref>
